newsitem.title: ITALY: Prodi says Italy sacrifices for EMU almost over.
newsitem.headline: Prodi says Italy sacrifices for EMU almost over.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi said in an interview published on Sunday that this was the last summer Italians would have to be prepared to make sacrifices to help their country enter European Economic and Monetary Union.

But he said there was no need for Italians to feel "anguish" over the difficulties the country will face this autumn, when the government is due to approve the 1998 budget and hopes to introduce cost-cutting pensions reform.
"This will be the last summer in which Italians will have to be prepared to make more sacrifices," Prodi was quoted as saying in an interview with the Il Tirreno newspaper.
"The road towards Europe is still uphill, but I really think that by next summer the downhill part will finally begin," he said.

Prodi has said often that Italy will be part of the single European currency at its launch in 1999. His government has embarked on an ambitious programme to cut the public sector deficit in order to meet criteria for entering EMU.
Italians have been asked to pay a one-off "Eurotax" to help the country get its public finances in order.
The government is currently engaged in negotiations with unions and business leaders aimed at securing agreement on a reduction in spending on state pensions.
"The race towards Europe is still very tough and requires a great commitment on everyone's part, even this coming autumn," Prodi said.
"But this should not cause any anguish. Everything has gone well so far and we have achieved important results. But woe to us if we are distracted," he said.

Prodi's comments in a television interview on Friday that the autumn would be a "very difficult" received wide coverage in the national media and his remarks in Sunday's newspaper interview appeared to be aimed at reassuring Italians.
The government is due to meet unions again on Tuesday on penions reforms before the summer break.
The 1998 budget has to be presented to parliament before the end of September and government officials are seeking an agreement on pensions reforms by then.
Communist Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti said after a meeting with Prodi on Thursday that the parliamentary majority supporting the centre-left government was "at risk."
Prodi relies upon Refoundation for a parliamentary majority and the two sides have had a strained relationship since Prodi took office in May 1996.
Bertinotti has warned that he is against cuts in pensions and health care and also has criticised some privatisation plans.
